summary: Describes the Simple Network Time Protocol, an adaptation of NTP for synchronizing computer clocks. It is a simpler way for clients that do not need all of NTP's machinery. It was replaced by RFC 1769.

plainLanguage.summary: SNTP lets a computer ask another for the time and set its clock, without the extra careful math that full NTP uses.

subtitle: A lightweight way to synchronize computer clocks over the network.

tldr.problem: Full NTP is complex and requires many algorithms and state management. Some applications just need to set their clock to within a second and do not need the extra machinery.
tldr.mechanism: SNTP uses the same message format as NTP but in a simpler request-reply mode: the client sends a message with nearly all fields set to zero, and the server replies with the current time. The client extracts the server's transmission timestamp and sets its clock.
tldr.outcome: SNTP provides millisecond-to-second level accuracy with minimal implementation complexity, making it suitable for devices that cannot run full NTP. RFC 1769 later refined the specification.

facts.label: Typical accuracy
facts.value: 1 to 50 milliseconds depending on network jitter

today: RFC 1361 is Informational and defines SNTP as specified. It was refined by RFC 1769 and later by RFC 5905 (which defines both NTP and SNTP variants). The protocol remains in use in embedded devices and simple network applications.

sections.title: Why Simpler Time Sync Matters
sections.content:
Full NTP, described in RFC 1305, uses complex algorithms to synchronize computer clocks across the Internet with high accuracy. It handles multiple possible synchronization sources, compensates for network jitter, and adjusts the clock rate to maintain long-term accuracy. This works well for servers, but full NTP is too heavy for many devices.

SNTP is an adaptation of NTP that drops the complexity when it is not needed. It works like a stateless remote-procedure call: the client asks the server for the time, the server replies, and the client extracts the answer. Accuracy is typically in the range of a second or a few milliseconds, depending on the network, which is sufficient for many applications. The RFC emphasizes that SNTP should be used only at the edges of the synchronization network—clients that only listen, and simple servers attached to a reliable time source such as a radio clock.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of NTP as a very careful teacher with lots of tricks to teach you the exact time. SNTP is a student asking the teacher once: "What time is it?" and trusting the answer.

sections.title: The NTP Message Format
sections.content:
SNTP reuses the NTP message format exactly: a 48-byte header followed by optional authentication. The header contains eight fields in the first four octets and four 64-bit timestamp fields.

The first octet holds three fields: Leap Indicator (2 bits, warns of a leap second), Version Number (3 bits, currently 3), and Mode (3 bits, indicating client, server, or broadcast). Below that are Stratum (the level of the source: 1 for primary, 2+ for secondary), Poll Interval (how often to poll, in powers of two), and Precision (the clock precision, also in powers of two). The next two fields, Root Delay and Root Dispersion, give the round-trip delay to the primary source and the maximum error, both in fixed-point seconds. Reference Identifier names the reference clock.

The four timestamp fields occupy 64 bits each. Reference Timestamp is when the clock was last set. Originate Timestamp is when the client sent the request. Receive Timestamp is when the server received it. Transmit Timestamp is when the server sent the reply. In SNTP, only the Transmit Timestamp matters to the client; it contains the server's time of day.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is a form you fill out. The client writes its name and "client mode" at the top and leaves everything else blank. The server fills in the current time in one field and sends it back.

sections.title: Client and Server Operation
sections.content:
An SNTP client is a stateless request-reply machine. It builds a message with all fields zeroed except the first octet, which has Leap Indicator set to zero, Version Number set (typically to 1 for compatibility), and Mode set to 3 (client). It sends this message to the server and waits for a reply. When the reply arrives, the client reads the Transmit Timestamp field, which contains the server's time in NTP format: a 64-bit number representing seconds and a fraction since midnight on 1 January 1900. The integer part is the seconds; the client can set its clock to that value or interpolate using the fraction for better accuracy.

The RFC recommends three error checks: if the Leap Indicator is 3 (alarm, meaning the server is not synchronized), if the Transmit Timestamp is zero (unsynchronized), or if the Stratum is 0, the client should disregard the reply. Otherwise, the time is usable.

An SNTP server is also stateless. It receives a message, ignores all fields except the first octet, and replies with a properly filled message. For a primary server connected to a radio clock, it sets Leap Indicator to 0 and Stratum to 1. It copies the Version Number and Poll fields from the request. It sets Mode to 4 (server) if the request was mode 3 (client), otherwise to 2 (symmetric passive). The Reference Timestamp, Receive Timestamp, and Transmit Timestamp are all set to the server's current time. The Originate Timestamp is copied unchanged from the request. The other fields are set to zero or to values reflecting the clock's precision and the radio clock's characteristics.
sections.plainLanguage: The client is like a student: it asks "What time is it?" and writes down the answer. The server is like a clock on the wall: whenever anyone asks, it says the current time.

sections.title: How Time is Represented
sections.content:
NTP and SNTP timestamps use a special 64-bit format: the first 32 bits are the integer part (seconds) and the last 32 bits are the fractional part. The value represents the number of seconds since midnight on 1 January 1900, using a fixed-point representation. This format allows for convenient arithmetic and has a precision of about 200 picoseconds, more than adequate for any practical timekeeping application.

The RFC notes an important quirk: since 1968, the most significant bit of the integer part (the sign bit in some representations) has been set, indicating the time is after 1900. The 64-bit field will overflow some time in 2036. The RFC suggests that when this happens, external metadata will be needed to distinguish times relative to 1900 from times relative to 2036. By convention, an all-zero timestamp is treated as "invalid".
sections.plainLanguage: The timestamp is like writing the date as a big number. NTP writes it in a special way that makes math easy and lets it be very, very precise—down to less than a millionth of a millionth of a second.

sections.title: When to Use SNTP
sections.content:
SNTP is intended for the edges of a time-synchronization network. SNTP clients are appropriate for devices that only receive time updates from servers, such as personal computers, workstations, or network appliances. SNTP servers should only be deployed at the root of the synchronization tree, directly connected to a reliable primary time source such as a radio clock. The RFC strongly cautions that the full redundancy, diverse paths, and crafted algorithms of a complete NTP implementation are needed to ensure the highest reliability, and that SNTP servers should be used only when an organization has a single, highly reliable reference clock and accepts the risks of lost synchronization if that clock fails.

Because SNTP discards most of the NTP header fields and does not maintain state, it cannot participate in the hierarchical, self-healing synchronization structure that full NTP supports. If an SNTP server becomes unsynchronized, it will immediately start serving incorrect time. If an SNTP client fails to receive a reply, it simply cannot update its clock. Therefore, SNTP is best suited to environments where time synchronization requirements are modest and the infrastructure is tightly controlled.
sections.plainLanguage: SNTP is for simple setups. Use it when you have one good clock and just want other computers nearby to match it. Do not use it if you need a big, reliable time network that can heal itself when clocks break.

fields.name: Leap Indicator
fields.desc: Warning of leap second: 0 = no warning, 3 = unsynchronized.

fields.name: Poll Interval
fields.desc: Maximum time between polls (power of 2, in seconds).

fields.name: Precision
fields.desc: Local clock precision (power of 2, in seconds).
